title: A prayer to see virtues
hookLine: Rebbe Elimelech's prayer asks to see the virtues of others, not their faults
carry: pray to see others' virtues, not their faults
tomorrow: under all the layers, what's left that never got dirty?

lines: A FACE IN A CROWD, IN A BLINK.
cards: A camera can pick one face out of a crowd in a blink. Picking out what's good in that face takes longer.

Rabbi Elimelech of Lizhensk, the Hasidic master known as Rebbe Elimelech, wrote a short prayer to be said before the daily prayers, and yes, it asks exactly that. It's not a long prayer, and it isn't abstract.
Among its requests: put it in our hearts that each of us sees the virtues of others, and not their faults.

teach.b: The prayer goes further than politeness. It asks that people speak with one another in a way that is upright before God, and that no hatred of one person for another rise in the heart.
It's a request, not an order, and it's said in the plural: us, each of us, all of us together. Rebbe Elimelech seems to know you can't simply decide to see differently, so he asks for help.
Faults are loud; they announce themselves. Virtues are often quiet, and you have to be looking for them.

And notice where it sits: before the morning prayers, as if a person can't stand before God well while still keeping score on everyone else. Now the week that led here. A wrestler who wins because he comes glad.
A rebbe hunting for one good point.
An hour alone, in your own words. Seven beggars, each flaw opening on a gift. A son who waited too long.
A rabbi who argued the people's case in heaven.

teach.h: PRAY TO SEE OTHERS' VIRTUES, NOT THEIR FAULTS.
teach.b: And a prayer to see the virtues. Seven days of later voices, one thread running through them: look again, and look kindly, at others and at yourself.

how: Rebbe Elimelech's prayer before prayer is printed in some prayer books and said by many Hasidim before the morning service, asking to see the virtues of others and to be free of hatred.

o: a blessing said on seeing a wise and learned person
asking to see the good in others, and not their faults
listing your own good deeds out loud before you pray

games.q: a week of later voices — tap the pairs.
p: the good point, and an hour alone
asked to see virtues, not faults

s: seeing the virtues means pretending people have no faults
the prayer knows faults are there; it asks to see the virtues first.
Rebbe Elimelech's prayer is said before the daily prayers
a prayer before prayer: you clear the score before you stand before God.
the prayer orders people to stop judging each other
it's a request for help: put it in our hearts to see the virtues.

games.q: after one class, a new teacher seems strict and unfair. a friend wants to start a group chat about him. what would Rebbe Elimelech's prayer ask first?
o: to see his virtues before deciding about his faults.
to see clearly which of his faults to report.
to stop thinking about the teacher at all.
games.why: the prayer asks to see the virtues of others and not their faults, and that no hatred rise between people.

practice: Bring one person to mind, someone close or someone hard. Count their virtues on your fingers, slowly, one for each breath: a skill, a kindness, a way they show up.
If the person is a hard one, the first virtue may take a while; let it. When you run out, start again from the first and see whether a new one comes.

wordCard.voice: See the virtues: from Rebbe Elimelech's prayer before prayer. Asking to see the good in others, and not their faults. The last word of the week.

orig.note: Hebrew: a virtue, a good quality; the same word also means a step up.

carryVoice: Here it is, folded small: pray to see others' virtues, not their faults. Seven days of teachers in one request. A good week to you.

sources.ref: Tefillah Kodem ha-Tefillah, the prayer before prayer of Rabbi Elimelech of Lizhensk (to see the virtues of our fellows and not their faults; to speak uprightly; that no hatred arise between people)
